entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 9 (Chasepoint, n1-3)

entries.wrong: Timber taken off a neighbour's sand is forbidden to everyone on this coast. Each family guards its own sand, a hereditary right handed down for longer than anyone can say.
entries.right: Take timber off a neighbour's sand and you will hear about it from every family on this coast. Each guards its own stretch, as their grandparents did. What the Southern Sea breaks comes ashore on the beach south of this stage.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 10 (Chasepoint, n1)

entries.wrong: I will not say which claim is better. Both houses trade with me on market days.
entries.right: Two houses claim the keeper's chair, each by blood. Pay for the chair stopped two centuries back. Both buy from me, so I will not say whose claim is better.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 11 (Chasepoint, n1-2)

entries.wrong: Quiet costs you a plank of good timber now.
entries.right: I saw that. Keep off my stretch of the shore.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 12 (Chasepoint, n1-2)

entries.wrong: Planks first ... Can you carry? The rest I buy cheap.
entries.right: Planks first, hauled up the beach when the sea pulls back. The rest I buy cheap, from whoever drags it up.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 13 (Chasepoint, n1-2)

entries.wrong: ... Did you meet fellrunners on the way here?
entries.right: Fellrunners in the scrub are worse than the marsh rats that chew my bedding at night. Stay on the path and out of the scrub.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 14 (Chasepoint, n1-3)

entries.tell: direction or distance against the road
entries.note: unnamed town, no direction or time
entries.wrong: The town is close, along the path beyond the yard gate. Fourth Stage is far.
entries.right: The old capital is a short walk west. Fourth Stage is east, a long way round by the causeway.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 15 (Chasepoint, n1-3)

entries.wrong: ... Look close, then.
entries.right: Soldiers built this stage for travellers. We put the reed on when the tiles went.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 16 (Chasepoint, n1-3)

entries.tell: a thing named so the player cannot place it
entries.wrong: ... Follow the tar smell and you find the timber stacks.
entries.right: East along the road is Fourth Stage, the next stage along the road. West is the old capital, near enough that I have walked it in the cool before work. The sea is two fields south, behind the scrub.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 17 (Chasepoint, n1-4)

entries.tell: a thing named so the player cannot place it
entries.wrong: ... to dry through the damp middle.
entries.right: I rinse the salt out of every coil and hang it in the old stable. Thirty, I make it. The stall writes twenty-nine.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 18 (Chasepoint, n1)

entries.wrong: ... Have you walked down there yet?
entries.right: Name any plank and I can tell you which ship it came off, once the families have hauled it up from the sea to the south and I have read the boards. The old stable holds the drying rope.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 19 (Chasepoint, n2)

entries.tell: direction or distance against the road
entries.note: town unnamed; west/south-west inconsistent with n1
entries.wrong: Go south-west for the town; it takes minutes on foot.
entries.right: The old capital is a few minutes' walk, south-west. Fourth Stage is east.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 20 (Chasepoint, n2)

entries.wrong: Have you a net that needs mending? I name one price for it, in drakes.
entries.right: I mend net. Torn lengths reach my rack once the tide is done with them. I name one price for each, in drakes.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 21 (Chasepoint, n1-4)

entries.wrong: ... Where no court sits, the marsh itself is the only law. Would you call that debt fair to a baby?
entries.right: A man takes a debt he cannot clear. It ties him to labour until the sum is paid. That bond is the Owing. It began as a few months of work as punishment. Now the paper is sold on and handed down, so a child can be born owing a sum he never signed. Where there is no court, that is the law.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 22 (Rose, tag-keeper)

entries.wrong: Have you come about one of the dead, friend?
entries.right: Have you come about one of the dead?
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 23 (Rose, tag-keeper)

entries.tell: direction or distance against the road
entries.note: no real exit; same as the other three
entries.wrong: The Rose lies along the Prison road in one direction. The villages lie along it in the other.
entries.right: The Prison road runs past this rise. The Rose lies down it one way, the villages the other. The track below my door goes on to Murkwood Verge, a short walk south-east.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 24 (Rose, tag-keeper)

entries.note: cheer contradicts the recorded sour dissent; exclamation
entries.wrong: Hard walking, but I would do it again tomorrow! ...
entries.right: Hard walking. The work earns me no thanks. The Rose releases its dead once the Chainbreakers have paid. Then I carry each one to its own tree, since bones laid in the dirt beside it may still reach home.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 25 (Rose, carrier)

entries.wrong: Thatch, hut, fire basin. Dry ground!
entries.right: A shelter, a hut, a brazier, on the only dry ground for a way round. The dead change hands here. I wrap them.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 26 (Rose, carrier)

entries.note: the dissent (families at their worst) is not voiced; "one pair" odd
entries.wrong: Ux-Vakka has the hut. The families stand in the door counting coins while one pair haggle over their dead.
entries.right: Ux-Vakka keeps the hut and writes every coin down. The families stand in the doorway counting out coins over their own dead. I wrap what they sold me and do not look at them.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 27 (Rose, carrier)

entries.note: closing question; the same two ends
entries.wrong: ... Is it the Rose you want?
entries.right: Follow the Prison road; I know every soft patch of it. One end reaches the Rose, the other the villages. For the North Stage take the track east, then north, then west; each leg is a short walk.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 28 (Rose, carrier)

entries.wrong: My feet know this road better than any map! ... on its dry bank
entries.right: Imperial crews cut the Prison road with the Border road beside it, then raised a waystation called the Mile House. The Tag House stands on a dry rise by the Prison road. I rest there. People still use the old names.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 29 (Rose, carrier)

entries.note: "citizen" is an Imperial word in an Argonian mouth
entries.wrong: Mind the bundles, citizen.
entries.right: Mind the bundles, stranger.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 30 (Rose, carrier)

entries.note: contradicts the same speaker's refusal to say "prison"
entries.wrong: ... an old prison of the Empire that now shelters whole families who call it home.
entries.right: Three rivers join at the lake city of Blackrose. A day's march off lies the Rose. The Empire filled it once. Whole families call it home now.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 31 (Rose, rose-family-2)

entries.wrong: The Empire put up a prison here once and filled it. ... We will not call our home a prison.
entries.right: The Empire filled the Rose once. Three generations of my family have been born in it since. Say prison in front of us and you are corrected before you finish. No fee here is more resented than the carriage charge.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 32 (Rose, rose-family-2)

entries.wrong: Three days our family has sat on that bench ... Would you wait so long on a payment you hate?
entries.right: Our family has sat on that bench all day for our aunt, over a payment we hate. The Empire made the Rose a prison. Three generations of us were born in it. We do not call it one.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 33 (Rose, rose-family)

entries.wrong: He has not sat down with us in all that time. ... Before that, I trust them hardly at all.
entries.right: Ux-Vakka the keeper writes each line fairly. Okan-Sei, who wraps our dead, comes from the villages and stares at a family still waiting. We wait at the door till the pen stops. Once the coin is down I trust the villages a little.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 34 (Rose, rose-family)

entries.wrong: Last week I spent a full morning settling a feud over whose pennant hangs lowest on the mast.
entries.right: Boats that haul goods round the river mouths or down the shore all sail under the Reed-Sail Compact: the guild of ferries, routes and hands, from the smallest punt to the biggest barge. Raiders sail with us. The Salt-Teeth fly the same mark as honest crews.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 35 (Lighter, flotilla-speaker)

entries.note: list of unrelated ideas; cooking line is also the lighterman's
entries.wrong: ... Neighbours here I know by their cooking before their faces.
entries.right: Three posts run the row and the Compact fills them: speaker, master of the lighters, purser. I hold the first. When the town demanded licences for jobs its own men never touched, the harbour sat shut a fortnight.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 36 (Lighter, flotilla-speaker)

entries.note: the third retelling of the strike
entries.wrong: Once the row did stop the port over a licence, a fortnight of idle hulls. ...
entries.right: I speak for the hulls whenever Lilmoth sends a letter. A hull stays tied until I nod. The vote to stop the port was mine to put, from this bow, with the whole row watching.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 37 (Lighter, flotilla-speaker)

entries.wrong: Are you walking? ...
entries.right: Passengers can board a hull from this pier, whether it sails for Archon or the far moorings. The big merchantman has bunks if night catches you. Walkers take the plank stage out over the reeds to the track into town.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 38 (Lighter, flotilla-speaker)

entries.wrong: Her captain glares at the town he cannot reach. I take the longest glare. Our berths sit outside the customs line.
entries.right: We call the small boats that fetch freight from far-anchored ships lighters. Lilmoth has no berth deep enough for a big hull, so a merchantman lies at her cable well out on the water and we go to her.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 39 (Lighter, lighterman)

entries.wrong: A merchant in town cannot land a single sack unless all four hulls agree to carry it.
entries.right: Each of the four hulls shelters its own crew, who eat, sleep and quarrel on the same decks. The Compact, our guild, gives out offices called posts. Three sit here and I fill one. The speaker, Opens-The-Books, fills another. Ninx-Ossa the purser the last.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 40 (Lighter, lighterman)

entries.wrong: Berths stay free of brawls that way.
entries.right: The Compact sets each crew's share, the cut of a route's takings it draws, so no crew undercuts another.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 41 (Lighter, lighterman)

entries.wrong: I will boast that it came back sharper.
entries.right: Umbriel, the flying city, destroyed Lilmoth in 4E 48 and the port was built back smaller. Merchants sit on the council that rules it now. Lilmoth stands over shallows, so a big vessel anchors far out while small craft like mine carry the loads ashore. Who took which side that year is not mine to tell.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 42 (Lighter, lighterman)

entries.wrong: Is it the anchorage you want, or Archon? ...
entries.right: I run the anchorage lighter myself and cast off at the turn of the water. Boats for Archon push off from this pier too, though other masters work them. The stage behind me meets the Lilmoth track.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 43 (Lighter, lighterman)

entries.wrong: ... Tariff means the tax a city charges on cargo as it arrives.
entries.right: Any traveller carrying the fare can sleep in my bunks down in the hold. Goods from the ship's stores I sell untaxed, so the price runs lower. Most of my day goes on writing every crate that comes aboard or leaves into the ship's books.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 44 (Lighter, purser)

entries.note: same three-step explainer as speaker and lighterman
entries.wrong: The council once proposed to license the lighters. Every crew stopped for two weeks. That stoppage is how the Compact keeps its monopoly ...
entries.right: I keep the books, so I know the shares. Each crew works the slice of a route the Compact gives it and no other. The Compact holds its monopoly by stopping work, as it did for two weeks when the council wanted licences.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 45 (Lighter, purser)

entries.wrong: ... The hands wait.
entries.right: A foot dangled off the pier edge draws osheeja gar or slaughterfish. I have seen it twice and not made the joke.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 46 (Lighter, purser)

entries.wrong: Want to cross over? ...
entries.right: Passengers for Archon or the anchorage board at this pier. Walking, step onto the landing stage at the bank end of the pier. The city track runs on from it.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 47 (Lighter, purser)

entries.wrong: ... Do you want the pier or the track first?
entries.right: Sailings for Archon and the anchorage start at the pier. Walking instead, cross the reeds on the plank stage and the city track begins past its far end.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 48 (Lighter, n1)

entries.wrong: The Reed-Sail Compact, a trading guild, owns every leading place on our crews.
entries.right: The Reed-Sail Compact, the guild of the boat crews, holds every leading post here. The council pressed for licences once, but every crew downed its lines for a fortnight.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 49 (Lighter, n1-2)

entries.note: route off the graph; closing question
entries.wrong: ... follow the road toward Lilmoth, then walk a short dry way south. ... Are you bound for Archon, or only the yard?
entries.right: Archon crews cast off here. For Under-Yard, cross the landing stage and take the track south, a short walk. The yard stands at its end.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 50 (Lighter, n1-2)

entries.wrong: ... Are you looking for passage out to one of the ships?
entries.right: Big ships cannot tie up in Lilmoth, there being no dock for them. They sit in the bay and small craft ferry the cargo ashore. I coil rope from dawn on one of those craft.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 51 (Lighter, n1-3)

entries.tell: direction or distance against the road
entries.note: gives the way to the pier the player is already at; drops the boats
entries.wrong: Follow the planks over the reeds from the end of the Lilmoth track until the pier stands in front of you.
entries.right: Take the planks over the reeds and you meet the Lilmoth track at the far end. Boats for Archon and the anchorage leave from this pier.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 52 (Lighter, n1-3)

entries.wrong: ... where a jaw beetle glowers at everyone and sulks until fight day.
entries.right: I like the box by my bunk best, where my jaw beetle waits for the fights at Archon.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 53 (Lighter, n1-4)

entries.wrong: He's in the box by the bunk.
entries.right: Ojel, come and see him. He is in the box by the bunk.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 54 (Lighter, n1-4)

entries.wrong: I'm off my turn. Ask away.
entries.right: I am off my turn. Ask away.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 55 (Lighter, n1)

entries.tell: a thing named so the player cannot place it
entries.wrong: The boards are slick with fish scales each morning ...
entries.right: The boards are slick every morning. I have sat down on them harder than I like to say.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 56 (Lighter, n2)

entries.note: closing question; same frame as n1-3, n1-4 and Chasepoint n1-2
entries.wrong: ... Has anyone called you that yet? It simply means outsiders.
entries.right: Lukiul is a cruel word, a slur the An-Xileel made for Argonians hatched beyond Black Marsh who cannot hear the Hist. Ojel only means outsider. Clerks, sailors and traders from every shore answer to it without a flicker.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 57 (Lighter, n2)

entries.note: restates n1-3 and n2; "carries no insult" is the pool's
entries.wrong: I flinch at lukiul. ... We call outsiders ojel. It is a word that carries no insult. I use it freely on the quay all day long.
entries.right: I flinch at lukiul. The An-Xileel made it to jeer at Argonians raised abroad, some of whom cannot hear the Hist at all. Ojel is only what we call outsiders. I say it all day on the quay.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 58 (Lighter, n1-4)

entries.note: same answer as n1, n1-3, n1-4
entries.wrong: Lighter work is two jobs. The deckhand bails the boat dry between runs, then hauls cargo up the side of a deep ship. ...
entries.right: Between runs I bail. At the anchorage, I haul cargo up the side of whatever ship is lying out there. No dock in Lilmoth takes them, so the lighter goes out every day.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 59 (Lighter, n1-2)

entries.wrong: ... on the first morning of the new rule. I coiled rope on the pier and watched the ships sit in the bay.
entries.right: The council wanted every crew to buy a licence, so every crew tied up together. Two weeks the port sat idle. The ships sat out in the bay.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch C, FIX 60 (Lighter, n1-3)

entries.note: Contradicts no central doctrine; invented scolding
entries.wrong: Taking a life is held to be his work too. The order faults anyone who reads it otherwise. ... as an acolyte learned when scolded before everyone.
entries.right: Sithis is the void god. All change is his. Dying is a change. We mourn our dead, then let them go.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 1 (Teeth, n2 (Wuleen-Wai))

entries.wrong: ...The mourners weep at the landing. Then the rite resumes at the next lamp.
entries.right: The clergy teach that a death is one more change. All change is Sithis's, the void god. The dead are mourned, then let go.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 2 (Teeth, n2-3 (Xal-Tei))

entries.wrong: ...At the last rite, green crept back over a tooth cleaned that morning.
entries.right: The temple stays as it is below the waterline. We scrub above it, nothing more. Waist-deep for hours, my legs go numb.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 3 (Teeth, n2)

entries.note: Contradicts waist-deep in the record and n2
entries.wrong: ...while the band wades the shallows, knee high, through every rite.
entries.right: while the band wades the shallows, waist-deep, through every rite.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 4 (Teeth, n2-4 (Teeb-Shaal))

entries.wrong: Watching, carrying and scrubbing together make the daily rite.
entries.right: Watching and carrying go on until it ends. It is cold.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 5 (Teeth, n2-3 and n2-4)

entries.note: Seventh copy of one doctrine sentence; "turns that wheel" is resonance
entries.wrong: Our dead are mourned, then released without wrong. The priests say dying only changes a thing. The void god Sithis turns that wheel for all of us.
entries.right: The priests say a death is a change. All change is Sithis's, the void god. We mourn, then let go. That is all I know of it. I scrub.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 6 (Teeth, the-one (Nesh-Katta))

entries.note: Boats not in any record; the way in is the pilgrim way
entries.wrong: Another boat. Yours?" / "I watched your boat tie up." / "No boats on the water tonight, friend." / "Fourth boat today." / "Boat on the water!
entries.right: Another pilgrim. On your own?" / "I watched you come up the steps." / "No pilgrims on the steps tonight, friend." / "Fourth pilgrim today." / "Pilgrim on the steps!
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 7 (Teeth, n2-3)

entries.wrong: ...the largest temple to Sithis in all Murkmire; those who tried to number its stones gave up before noon.
entries.right: What offering have you brought? The Nisswo who tend this colonnade have never settled why it was raised. It is the largest temple to Sithis in all Murkmire.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 8 (Teeth, nisswo-teeth (Ohl-Nakka))

entries.tell: a thing named so the player cannot place it
entries.wrong: Fourth Stage lies along the old road. Leave the worn way and follow its track from the end.
entries.right: Fourth Stage is a short walk north, along the old road. Take the track at the end of the pilgrim way.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 9 (Teeth, nisswo-teeth)

entries.note: Bearing no record holds; contradicts n1, n2, n2-4
entries.wrong: Fourth Stage is close. Leave the pilgrim way on the north-west track, then turn east.
entries.right: Fourth Stage is close. North, a short walk from the end of the pilgrim way.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 10 (Teeth, the-one)

entries.note: Invented rule; fact-stack with appositive gloss
entries.wrong: Leeches crowd the shallows ... so I wade out by day only. Swamp jellies drift in on the tide after dark. A voriplasm, a hungry jelly-like thing that strips anything dropped in the water, lives in the drowned room below the floor. Down there I go in company or not at all.
entries.right: Leeches crowd the shallows round the teeth and swamp jellies drift in on the tide. The voriplasm lives in the drowned room below the floor. It strips whatever falls into it. I stay away from that room.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 11 (Teeth, n2-2 (Sal-Xeek))

entries.note: Cut-Rope is a band of tribeless Naga, not a village
entries.wrong: Raiders from Cut-Rope, a raiding village down the track, kill walkers out on the paths.
entries.right: Cut-Rope's raiders, a band of tribeless Naga down the track, kill walkers out on the paths.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 12 (Naga, jeen-ozzu (n2))

entries.tell: a thing named so the player cannot place it
entries.wrong: In the evenings, the drum sounds loud across the water.
entries.right: The smoke from the racks lies low over the water in the evenings.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 13 (Naga, jeen-ozzu)

entries.wrong: The best are set aside for trading with the river clans later.
entries.right: The best are set aside for trade.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 14 (Naga, bux-xeek (n2-2))

entries.note: Im-Jei's argument is nowhere; census opener
entries.wrong: Okan-Leel is slow before noon while Im-Jei argues with every post he stands.
entries.right: Heita-Kai is the lieutenant. Okan-Leel is slow before noon. The settled tribes blame all of us for the killings other camps do along the walker paths.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 15 (Naga, bux-xeek)

entries.wrong: ...The road to that camp runs past our gate. One of the band stands between the totems there in turns.
entries.right: The track to that camp runs past our gate, where one of the band stands between the totems.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 16 (Naga, heita-kai (n1))

entries.note: Census plus the five-way role list
entries.wrong: Six of us work turns, myself and five others. Whoever has the bend whistles when a stranger comes up the wet ground below. Another tends the hides by the embers while the rest doze and a third minds the totems by the gate.
entries.right: The bend is mine this watch. A walker rounds it, I whistle. The camp is up. We swap bend, fire and gate in turns. Whoever has the fire smokes the hides.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 17 (Naga, im-jei (n2-5))

entries.wrong: I like the fire. There one of us smokes hides while the others rest in the tent. Another sits up on the scaffold ... A third stands by the totems at the gate. We all change places in turns.
entries.right: The fire is my post and the tent is my bed. I smoke hides while the others sleep. When my turn to sleep comes I go down like a stone. We change places in turns.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 18 (Naga, okan-leel (n2-3))

entries.note: Fourth copy of the danger stack; appositive gloss
entries.wrong: I stay clear of the water below the camp. A crocodile dens there with hackwings and death hoppers in the reeds. Cut-Rope's raiders hunt these same stretches and kill walkers, then the settled tribes, the ones with villages and hearths, look at us and say the blood is ours. Kill one walker and his tribe comes down on the camp, so we lift the cargo and nothing else.
entries.right: I stay clear of the water. Crocodile. Hackwings and death hoppers in the reeds. Cut-Rope's raiders do the killing and the settled tribes say the blood is ours. Ours! We lift cargo and let them walk.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 19 (Naga, okan-leel)

entries.note: Assumes the player's origin; two glosses in one run
entries.wrong: ...Hatched in a far land, you cannot hear them, the great trees we call the Hist. We call outsiders ojel, anyone from beyond Black Marsh. It is no insult.
entries.right: Ojel is what we call anyone from beyond Black Marsh. A plain word, no insult. Lukiul is the insult. The An-Xileel use it for Argonians who took foreign ways. An ojel hatched in a far land cannot hear the Hist, the great trees.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 20 (Naga, guul-teeba (n2-4))

entries.tell: direction or distance against the road
entries.note: Kilometre breaks the z3 rule; "inland" against the beach landing
entries.wrong: Go north-west on the Long road and you reach the inland village of Portdun Mont after half a kilometre.
entries.right: Go north-west on the Long road and you reach Portdun Mont in ten minutes' walk.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 21 (Pearl, n1 (Xuth-Ra))

entries.wrong: ...Walkers go along the Long road, the track inland, heading north and west for half a kilometre.
entries.right: By sea, run west along the coast from the spit until a village shows on its rise. That is Portdun Mont. Archon is a harbour farther along the shore. On foot, the Long road, north-west, ten minutes.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 22 (Pearl, n2 (Deeka-Kaya))

entries.note: The divers go home to Archon each night
entries.wrong: Archon is the big port, far past anywhere I have walked. First go west by the shoreline to the landing under Portdun Mont.
entries.right: Archon is the big port, where we go home at night. West by the shoreline to the landing below Portdun Mont, then onward.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 23 (Pearl, n1-3 (Guul-Vakka))

entries.wrong: ...My own lot I know well. Could you tell mine from the next? I know the rest by number.
entries.right: Down past the shelf, buoys float over numbered lots of seabed. Mine I know by the bottom itself. The rest I know by number.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 24 (Pearl, n1-3)

entries.wrong: I know of the other families what their tally book lists. That is the book where the pay and the deaths are written, with shells taken and drownings. Every lot passes by inheritance...
entries.right: I know the other families by what the tally book says of them. Pay and deaths, side by side. Every lot passes from parent to child inside one family. We all share the tenders out on the water.
entries.round: 2.6 corpus read batch D, FIX 25 (Pearl, n1-3)

entries.wrong: Lots are inherited so I open shells at the table where the catch is graded by size. I know each net.
entries.right: Lots are inherited, family to family. I open shells at the grading table. I know each net that comes into the shed.
